steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on FedRDMA, a system that uses chunked RDMA transmission to reduce communication cost in cross-silo federated LLM training. Explain why cross-silo FedLLM matters, why communication over WANs is the bottleneck, why plain RDMA doesn't work on WANs, and list our contributions.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
## Cross-silo FedLLM
- LLMs: remarkable proficiency on generic ML tasks
- many companies developing own LLMs: medical (computational phenotyping, medical information extraction), financial (data mining, generation from text)
- data privacy concerns + isolated training data -> FL = predominant way to train LLMs collaboratively w/o sharing raw data ("FedLLM")
- our focus: cross-silo FedLLM; clients = powerful industrial servers, high bandwidth + computational resources

## Cross-silo FedLLM Communication Overhead
- better GPUs -> less computation overhead; communication overhead on WANs still formidable even w/ high bandwidth
- example: full-tuning GPT-2 (117M parameters), two NVIDIA A800 80G GPUs, 10Gbps -> 45.9s per round for model weights, >44.97% of total FL time
- causes: repeated memory copies + context switchings (TCP protocol stack), inherent WAN delay -> § 2.1

## Communication-Efficient RDMA
- Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA): recently widely used to cut communication overhead in LAN distributed ML
- direct transfer between memories of two RDMA-enabled servers, bypass CPU + OS kernel; up to 98.8% less overhead (§ 2.2)
- but needs lossless network -> nearly impractical on WANs
- packet loss/delays common on WANs -> many retransmissions, unacceptable for RDMA -> smaller improvement or even transmission failures

## Our Solution: FedRDMA
- inspired by modular parameters in LLMs
- manage application layer traffic flow: small packets, chunked, sequential, smooth
- RDMA memory pool: in-place buffering, reversed receiving strategy, reassemble chunks
- contributions:
  - preliminary experiments: high communication overhead despite high bandwidth/computation
  - FedRDMA system: chunked RDMA transmission + series of optimizations
  - implemented atop FATE (industrial FedLLM framework); up to 3.8 \times less communication time vs TCP-based FedLLM systems

steps.text:
## Cross-silo FedLLM

Large Language Models (LLMs) are very good at handling generic machine learning tasks. Because of this, a lot of companies have started to develop their own LLMs for different applications. In the medical field this includes computational phenotyping and medical information extraction, and in the financial sector it includes data mining and generation from text. But there are concerns about data privacy, and the training data is often isolated, so federated learning (FL) has become the main method for training LLMs together without sharing the raw data. This is called FedLLM. In this study we look at cross-silo FedLLM, where the clients are powerful industrial servers that have high bandwidth and a lot of computational resources.

## Cross-silo FedLLM Communication Overhead

Getting more powerful GPUs can reduce the computation overhead, but the communication overhead on WANs is still a big challenge, even when the bandwidth is high. For example, if we federate full-tuning of the GPT-2 model (117M parameters) with two NVIDIA A800 80G GPUs and 10Gbps bandwidth, it still takes 45.9s per round just to transfer the model weights. This is more than 44.97% of the total FL time. The delay comes from the TCP protocol stack, which causes repeated memory copies and context switchings, and also from the delay that the WAN itself has. We explain this more in § 2.1.

## Communication-Efficient RDMA
- Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA): recently widely used to cut communication overhead in LAN distributed ML
- direct transfer between memories of two RDMA-enabled servers, bypass CPU + OS kernel; up to 98.8% less overhead (§ 2.2)
- but needs lossless network -> nearly impractical on WANs
- packet loss/delays common on WANs -> many retransmissions, unacceptable for RDMA -> smaller improvement or even transmission failures

## Our Solution: FedRDMA
- inspired by modular parameters in LLMs
- manage application layer traffic flow: small packets, chunked, sequential, smooth
- RDMA memory pool: in-place buffering, reversed receiving strategy, reassemble chunks
- contributions:
  - preliminary experiments: high communication overhead despite high bandwidth/computation
  - FedRDMA system: chunked RDMA transmission + series of optimizations
  - implemented atop FATE (industrial FedLLM framework); up to 3.8 \times less communication time vs TCP-based FedLLM systems

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
## Cross-silo FedLLM

Large Language Models (LLMs) are very good at handling generic machine learning tasks. Because of this, a lot of companies have started to develop their own LLMs for different applications. In the medical field this includes computational phenotyping and medical information extraction, and in the financial sector it includes data mining and generation from text. But there are concerns about data privacy, and the training data is often isolated, so federated learning (FL) has become the main method for training LLMs together without sharing the raw data. This is called FedLLM. In this study we look at cross-silo FedLLM, where the clients are powerful industrial servers that have high bandwidth and a lot of computational resources.

## Cross-silo FedLLM Communication Overhead

Getting more powerful GPUs can reduce the computation overhead, but the communication overhead on WANs is still a big challenge, even when the bandwidth is high. For example, if we federate full-tuning of the GPT-2 model (117M parameters) with two NVIDIA A800 80G GPUs and 10Gbps bandwidth, it still takes 45.9s per round just to transfer the model weights. This is more than 44.97% of the total FL time. The delay comes from the TCP protocol stack, which causes repeated memory copies and context switchings, and also from the delay that the WAN itself has. We explain this more in § 2.1.

## Communication-Efficient RDMA

Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) is a technique that has recently become widely used for reducing communication overhead in distributed machine learning in local-area networks (LANs). RDMA can transfer data directly between the memories of two servers that are RDMA-enabled, and it bypasses the CPU and the OS kernel. As we show in § 2.2, this can reduce the communication overhead by up to 98.8%. The problem is that RDMA needs a lossless network environment to reach its potential, so it is almost impractical on WANs. Packet loss and delays happen a lot on WANs and they lead to many retransmissions, which RDMA cannot accept. So the performance improvement of RDMA gets smaller, or the transmission can even fail.

## Our Solution: FedRDMA

We propose FedRDMA, which was inspired by the modular parameters in LLMs. FedRDMA manages the traffic flow at the application layer by sending small packets in a chunked, sequential and smooth way. We also design a RDMA memory pool that uses in-place buffering and a reversed receiving strategy, so the chunks can be reassembled effectively and the performance is better. Our contributions are:

- We do preliminary experiments that show that cross-silo FedLLM still has high communication overhead, even though there is high bandwidth and a lot of computation resources.

- We propose FedRDMA, a cross-silo FedLLM system that is communication-efficient, with chunked RDMA transmission and a series of optimizations.

- We implement FedRDMA on top of FATE, an industrial FedLLM framework, and do extensive experiments that show it saves up to 3.8 \times communication time compared to FedLLM systems based on TCP.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
## Cross-silo FedLLM

Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable proficiency in handling generic machine learning tasks [1,2,3,4,5]. This has led many companies to develop their own LLMs for various applications, including computational phenotyping and medical information extraction in the medical field [6,7], and data mining and generation from text in the financial sector [8,9]. Given concerns about data privacy [10] and the challenge of isolated training data [11,12], federated learning (FL) has become the predominant method for collaboratively training LLMs without sharing raw data, known as FedLLM [13,14,15,16,17]. This study focuses on cross-silo FedLLM, where the clients are powerful industrial servers with high bandwidth and computational resources.

## Cross-silo FedLLM Communication Overhead

While acquiring more powerful GPUs can reduce computation overhead, the communication overhead on WANs remains a formidable challenge, even with high bandwidth. For instance, when federating full-tuning of the GPT-2 model (117M parameters) [18] with two NVIDIA A800 80G GPUs and 10Gbps bandwidth, transferring the model weights still takes 45.9s per round, which is more than 44.97% of the total FL time. This delay is caused by repeated memory copies and context switchings in the TCP protocol stack and by the inherent delay of the WAN itself, as we elaborate in § 2.1.

## Communication-Efficient RDMA

Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) is a technique that has recently become widely used to reduce communication overhead in local-area network (LAN) distributed machine learning [19,20]. It transfers data directly between the memories of two RDMA-enabled servers, bypassing the CPU and OS kernel, which can reduce the communication overhead by up to 98.8% as shown in § 2.2. However, RDMA needs a lossless network environment to fulfill its potential, which makes it nearly impractical on WANs. Packet loss and delays are common on WANs and lead to numerous retransmissions, which RDMA cannot accept [21], diminishing RDMA's performance improvement or even causing transmission failures.

## Our Solution: FedRDMA

Inspired by the modular parameters in LLMs, we propose FedRDMA, which manages the application layer traffic flow by transferring small packets in a chunked, sequential, and smooth manner. To further improve performance, we design a RDMA memory pool with in-place buffering and a reversed receiving strategy to reassemble chunks effectively. Our contributions are as follows:

- • We conduct preliminary experiments showing that cross-silo FedLLM still suffers from high communication overhead, despite high bandwidth and computation resources.

- • We propose FedRDMA, a communication-efficient cross-silo FedLLM system featuring chunked RDMA transmission and a series of optimizations.

- • We implement FedRDMA atop the industrial FedLLM framework FATE and conduct extensive experiments showing it saves up to 3.8 \times communication time compared to TCP-based FedLLM systems.
